domain: The long-settled historical verdict that the 1970s British postal strike was 'won' by the unions — and how that consensus was assembled
topic: The long-settled historical verdict that the 1970s British postal strike was 'won' by the unions — and how that consensus was assembled

source.title: Patrick Cockburn: Leap in the Dark

movement.gist: Lay out the textbook-settled verdict: the 1971 postal strike, seven weeks long, ending in defeat on pay but victory in spirit — cited in labour histories, union folklore, and retrospectives as the moment postal workers' dignity was restored even though they lost the immediate claim; establish this as unquestioned common knowledge repeated across generations of accounts.

Trace how this verdict formed: not through contemporary assessment but through a handful of oral-history projects and a single influential 1985 union-commissioned retrospective pamphlet, whose framing was then recycled by subsequent labour historians who cited each other rather than primary strike-pay ledgers or Post Office board minutes.

Expose the flaw: the oral histories were collected almost entirely from strike organisers and shop stewards still active in the union in the 1980s, systematically excluding the majority who left postal work afterward, disproportionately older sorters and rural staff, whose absence silently tilted the 'moral victory' framing.

The verdict on the strike itself is not what's wrong or right — the real defect is that no one ever asked who was actually eligible to shape the memory in the first place, and that question belongs to archival sociology, not labour history.

primary.axis: whether the 1971 UK national postal strike was a labour victory or a labour defeat
poles: the strike broke the union and normalised concessionary bargaining
the strike is remembered as a heroic stand that shamed the Post Office into reform

secondary.axis: who gets to author the memory of an industrial dispute
poles: institutional and press archives compiled at the time

tension_system.interaction: the secondary tension explains why the primary one calcified into a verdict at all — the archive that won was the one that was easiest to retell

family_realization.note: Passage exhumes the 1971 postal strike verdict by dissecting HOW consensus formed (1985 oral histories, citation loops, survivor bias) rather than adjudicating win/loss. Author refuses 'opposite verdict,' displacing focus to archival selection itself. The autopsy is structural and complete.

ending_behavior.note: Final sentence: 'it is that selection, not the seven weeks, that we should have been studying' relocates inquiry from labour history to archival sociology. Aperture 'displaces' perfectly—reframes the proper object of study. Clean handover.

voice_consistency.note: Insider authority (trained on these books, absorbed verdict before weighing). Elegiac tone (smooth assurance, hall of mirrors). One stubborn particular: the uncatalogued ledgers a mile away. Uneven—some sentences epigrammatic, others workmanlike. Human texture present.

distractor_efficiency.note: Q1(C): premature_closure trap—natural question set up then refused. Q3(B,D): stance_misread traps—tempt conflation of reported vs. endorsed. Q4(A): stance_misread—author treats moral-victory reading as open, not privately held. Q5(A): adjacent_answer—loss already conceded. Traps are genuine.

explanation_quality.note: Every wrong option anchored to passage location and mechanism: 'citation circle is evidence for witness selection, not primary concern' (Q1A); 'author claims no irrecoverability; he says moral-victory reading may well be true' (Q2B); 'sample tilted does not mean defeat' (Q3A). Specific, not generic.

answers.reasoning: Passage concludes real object is studying how records select witnesses, not strike outcome.
Final sentence explicitly relocates inquiry to record's witness-selection process.
Author describes moral-victory reading as inherited belief, never endorses it as true.
Author refuses to convert evidentiary bias into opposite substantive verdict, staying methodologically cautious.
If sample were balanced, the selection-bias critique underlying the argument collapses.
Phrase shows many sources were really one recycled voice, setting up witness-selection point.
Generalizing the pattern to other disputes strengthens claim about selective witness survival mattering.
Text states oral histories drawn almost wholly from organisers and stewards still active fourteen years later.
